recipe.history:
Burrata is a relatively young cheese by the standards of Italian dairy tradition, originating in the Murgia plateau of Puglia in southern Italy sometime in the early twentieth century — most accounts place its invention around 1920 in the town of Andria, attributed to a cheesemaker named Lorenzo Bianchino at the Masseria Bianchino farm. The cheese was born from resourcefulness: the fresh mozzarella-making process produces irregular scraps of curd and cream that would otherwise go to waste, and Bianchino's solution was to fashion a thin pouch of hand-stretched mozzarella pasta filata and fill it with these scraps — the stracciatella — mixed with fresh cream. The result is a cheese that behaves unlike almost anything else: its exterior is composed and firm enough to hold a shape, but when cut or broken, it collapses inward and releases a river of warm, lush cream and soft curd that coats everything it touches. The name comes from the Italian word for 'buttered,' which understates the effect considerably.

Burrata arrived in the United States in the late 1990s and early 2000s, initially imported from Puglia and later produced domestically by artisan cheesemakers in California who recognized both the demand and the challenges of shipping such a delicate, short-lived cheese across an ocean. American chefs fell for it immediately and somewhat helplessly — it is difficult not to. By 2010 burrata had become a menu fixture at Italian-influenced restaurants across major cities, appearing on charcuterie boards, over roasted tomatoes, draped across pizza, and eventually landing on burgers as the artisan burger movement matured and chefs grew more willing to treat the format as a canvas for serious ingredients. The key discovery was that burrata's flowing cream interior functions as both cheese and sauce simultaneously, eliminating the need for any additional spread.

I had my first burrata at a tiny restaurant in the West Village where the menu described it only as 'burrata, tomato, olive oil,' and I ordered it without fully knowing what I was in for. The plate arrived looking almost sculptural — a white globe sitting in a shallow pool of the best olive oil I had ever tasted, surrounded by halved heirloom tomatoes in four colors. The server nodded at me to cut into it. I did, and watched the cream spill out slowly, almost reluctantly, like it knew what it was giving up. The flavor was so clean and so rich at the same time that I sat very still for a moment and said nothing. The person across from me asked if I was all right. I was more than all right. I had just understood something about what food could do when an ingredient is simply excellent and you get out of its way.

A medium-rare burger at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — and a whole burrata broken over its top are made for each other in a way that feels almost predetermined. The heat of the patty, rested and juicy, gently warms the cream of the burrata as it spreads across the surface, thinning it slightly into a silken sauce that mingles with the meat juices underneath. If you cook the patty to well-done, it has nothing to offer this partnership — the juice is gone, the fat is rendered out, and you are left with dry beef under a pool of cream that has nowhere to go and nothing to integrate with. The medium-rare patty is warm and giving; the burrata responds in kind. This is a burger that only works at the right temperature.
ingredients: 1 ball fresh burrata (4 oz / 113g), at room temperature
A handful of fresh basil leaves
Flaky sea salt and cracked black pepper for finishing
1 small garlic clove, minced to a paste
instructions: 1. Roast the cherry tomatoes: preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Toss cherry tomato halves with olive oil, balsamic vinegar, honey, salt, and pepper on a small baking sheet. Roast for 20 to 25 minutes until collapsed and caramelized. Set aside to cool slightly.
2. Make the basil aioli: combine mayonnaise, chopped basil, garlic paste, and lemon juice in a small bowl. Season with salt. Refrigerate until ready to use.
3. Remove the burrata from the refrigerator at least 30 minutes before serving so it reaches room temperature — cold burrata does not flow as freely and its flavor is muted when chilled.

4. Remove ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking. Form gently into a single patty about 4 inches in diameter and 3/4-inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper.
5. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat.
6. Place the patty in the pan and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes to build a deep, even crust.
7. Flip once. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes. Do NOT add cheese to the pan — the burrata will go on after assembly.
8. Check internal temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3 minutes.
9. Melt butter in a separate pan over medium heat. Toast the brioche bun cut-side down until golden, 1 to 2 minutes.
10. Spread basil aioli generously on both bun halves.
11. Place heirloom tomato slices on the bottom bun. Lay fresh basil leaves over the tomatoes.
12. Place the rested patty on top of the basil and tomato.
13. Spoon the balsamic-roasted cherry tomatoes over and around the patty.
14. Drizzle extra-virgin olive oil over the patty and toppings.
15. Place the whole burrata ball directly on top of the patty. Using two spoons or a knife, gently break it open so the cream and stracciatella spill over the burger.
16. Finish with a generous pinch of flaky sea salt and several cracks of black pepper over the burrata.
17. Close with the top bun and serve immediately before the burrata cools.
